question.knowledge_point: Inverting Affine Transformations Given in Matrix Form
question.problem:
The matrix form of the affine transformation $T$ is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 2 \\ 4 & -2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 7\end{aligned}].
$$

Find $a+b+c,$ given that the matrix form of the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ a & b\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ c\end{aligned}].
$$
question.worked_solution:
An affine transformation $T:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2}$ is a function of the form

$$
x=Au+b,
$$

where $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Reversing the action of $T,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}Au+b & =x \\ Au & =x-b \\ u & ={A}^{-1}(x-b).\end{aligned}
$$

The matrix form of $T$ gives us the following information:

$$
{{[\begin{aligned}-3 & 2 \\ 4 & -2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 7\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}
$$

Next, we calculate the inverse of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{-2\cdot (-3)-2\cdot 4}[\begin{aligned}-2 & -2 \\ -4 & -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{-2}[\begin{aligned}-2 & -2 \\ -4 & -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 2 & \frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u} & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 2 & \frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{A}^{-1}}\cdot ({{[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{x}-{{[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 7\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 2 & \frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 2 & \frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 7\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 2 & \frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}3 \\ \frac{5}{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 2 & \frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ -\frac{5}{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+b+c=2+\frac{3}{2}+(-\frac{5}{2})=1.
$$

$$
[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}a & -2 \\ -4 & b\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}4 \\ c\end{aligned}].
$$

An affine transformation $T:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2}$ is a function of the form

$$
x=Au+b,
$$

where $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

$$
\begin{aligned}Au+b & =x \\ Au & =x-b \\ u & ={A}^{-1}(x-b).\end{aligned}
$$

The matrix form of $T$ gives us the following information:

$$
{{[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -4 & 7\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -5\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{7\cdot 1-(-2)\cdot (-4)}[\begin{aligned}7 & 2 \\ 4 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{-1}[\begin{aligned}7 & 2 \\ 4 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-7 & -2 \\ -4 & -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

$$

question.knowledge_point: Inverting Affine Transformations Given in Parametric Form
question.problem:
The affine transformation $T$ is defined as

$$
x=2u-3v-4,\,y=2u-4v-5.
$$

Given that the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ of $T$ is

$$
u=2x+ay+b,\,v=x-y+c,
$$

what is the value of $a+b+c?$
question.worked_solution:
An affine transformation $T:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2}$ is a function of the form

$$
x=Au+b,
$$

where $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Reversing the action of $T,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}Au+b & =x \\ Au & =x-b \\ u & ={A}^{-1}(x-b).\end{aligned}
$$

So, writing our transformation in matrix form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2u-3v-4 \\ 2u-4v-5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2u-3v \\ 2u-4v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ -5\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ 2 & -4\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ -5\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we calculate the inverse of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{-4\cdot 2-(-3)\cdot 2}[\begin{aligned}-4 & 3 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{-2}[\begin{aligned}-4 & 3 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -\frac{3}{2} \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u} & ={{[\begin{aligned}2 & -\frac{3}{2} \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{A}^{-1}}\cdot ({{[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{x}-{{[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ -5\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -\frac{3}{2} \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x+4 \\ y+5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2\cdot (x+4)+(-\frac{3}{2})\cdot (y+5) \\ 1\cdot (x+4)+(-1)\cdot (y+5)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2x-\frac{3}{2}y+\frac{1}{2} \\ x-y-1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding components, the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ in coordinate form is

$$
u=2x+(-\frac{3}{2})y+\frac{1}{2},\,v=x-y+(-1).
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+b+c=-\frac{3}{2}+\frac{1}{2}+(-1)=-2.
$$

question.knowledge_point: Inverting Affine Transformations Given in Parametric Form
question.problem:
The affine transformation $T$ is defined as

$$
x=5v-7u+3,\,y=7v-10u+5.
$$

Given that the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ of $T$ is

$$
u=ax-5y+4,\,v=bx+cy+5,
$$

what is the value of $a+b+c?$
question.worked_solution:
An affine transformation $T:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2}$ is a function of the form

$$
x=Au+b,
$$

where $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Reversing the action of $T,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}Au+b & =x \\ Au & =x-b \\ u & ={A}^{-1}(x-b).\end{aligned}
$$

So, writing our transformation in matrix form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}5v-7u+3 \\ 7v-10u+5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-7u+5v \\ -10u+7v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 5\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}-7 & 5 \\ -10 & 7\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 5\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we calculate the inverse of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{7\cdot (-7)-5\cdot (-10)}[\begin{aligned}7 & -5 \\ 10 & -7\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}7 & -5 \\ 10 & -7\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u} & ={{[\begin{aligned}7 & -5 \\ 10 & -7\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{A}^{-1}}\cdot ({{[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{x}-{{[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 5\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}7 & -5 \\ 10 & -7\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x-3 \\ y-5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}7\cdot (x-3)+(-5)\cdot (y-5) \\ 10\cdot (x-3)+(-7)\cdot (y-5)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}7x-5y+4 \\ 10x-7y+5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding components, the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ in coordinate form is

$$
u=7x-5y+4,\,v=10x+(-7)y+5.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+b+c=7+10+(-7)=10.
$$

question.knowledge_point: Identifying the Types of Images Formed by an Affine Transformation
question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14097781/assets/1f550963f047a3860566564abc2cb1e9f3939125895912762ff751767ca55c57.png)

Consider the affine transformation $T,$ given by

$$
x=2u-v,\,y=4u-v+2.
$$

What would be the image of the pentagon shown above under the action of $T?$
question.worked_solution:
Recall that for any affine transformation 

$$
T:u⟶Au+b,
$$

where $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix and $u$ and $b$ are $2\times 1$ column vectors, we have one of the following three possibilities:

- If $T$ is non-singular, i.e., when $det(A)\ne 0,$ then the image of a two-dimensional object is a two-dimensional object. In particular, the image of a polygon with $n$ vertices is a polygon with $n$ vertices.

- If $T$ is singular, i.e., when $det(A)=0,$ we have two additional subcases:

- If $A$ has at least one nonzero entry, then the image of a two-dimensional object is a one-dimensional line segment.

- If $A$ is the zero matrix, then the image of a two-dimensional object is a point on the plane.

With that in mind, let's examine our transformation.

The given transformation can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2u-v \\ 4u-v+2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2u-v \\ 4u-v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 4 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the matrix representation of the linear transformation associated with $T$ is 
$A=[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 4 & -1\end{aligned}].$

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}det(T) & =|\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 4 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =2\cdot (-1)-4\cdot (-1) \\  & =2 \\  & \ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a non-singular matrix. 

Therefore, $T$ is invertible, and the image of the pentagon under the action of $T$ is a pentagon.

question.knowledge_point: Identifying the Boundary of a Set
question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14097897/assets/d3ded2a039746e3c8f7a7ee4afb70b0d697468d1aee8f0e9dab24b1ca87897d2.png)

Consider the set $A,$ shown above. The boundary of $A$ is given by

$$
∂A={(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,\,}.
$$

What is the missing expression?
question.worked_solution:
The boundary of a set $A,$ denoted $∂A,$ is the set that contains all the boundary points of $A.$

The set $A$ and its boundary $∂A$ are shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14097897/assets/d1946cea37f202705e6517ba760afa6617075f748901b10588ea98628a3e9e50.png)

From the diagram, the boundary points of $A$ lie on the parabola $2y={x}^{2}.$

Therefore, 

$$
∂A={(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,2y={x}^{2}\,}.
$$

question.knowledge_point: Identifying the Boundary of a Set
question.problem:
Consider the set $A,$ defined by 

$$
A={(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,-2y\ge {x}^{2}}.
$$

The boundary of $A$ is given by

$$
∂A={(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,}.
$$

What is the missing expression?
question.worked_solution:
The boundary of a set $A,$ denoted $∂A,$ is the set that contains all the boundary points of $A.$

The set $A$ and its boundary $∂A$ are shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14097897/assets/0fc95ee69ce7121c0cf8ae68029b135d9667f50275227d141f1d979f85408859.png)

From the diagram, the boundary points of $A$ lie on the  parabola $-2y={x}^{2}.$ 

Therefore,  

$$
∂A={(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,-2y={x}^{2}\,}.
$$

question.knowledge_point: Finding the Total Displacement of a Particle Given Its Velocity
question.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis and its velocity at time $t$ is given by $v(t)=2t-\sqrt{t}.$ What is the total displacement of the particle between $t=0$ and $t=9?$
question.worked_solution:
We find the total displacement by calculating the definite integral of the velocity.

Let $d$ be the total displacement. Then we have

$$
\begin{aligned}d & ={\int }_{0}^{9}(2t-\sqrt{t})\text{d}t \\  & ={({t}^{2}-\frac{2}{3}{t}^{3/2})|}_{0}^{9} \\  & =[(9)^{2}-\frac{2}{3}(9)^{3/2}]-[(0)^{2}-\frac{2}{3}(0)^{3/2}] \\  & =81-18-0 \\  & =63.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the total displacement between $t=0$ and $t=9$ is $63.$

question.knowledge_point: Finding the Final Position of a Particle
question.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis and its velocity at time $t>0$ is given by $v(t)={e}^{2-t}.$ At time $t=1$ the particle is located at the position $x=e.$ What is the position of the particle at time $t=2?$
question.worked_solution:
The position of the particle at $t=2$ is equal to its position at $t=1$ plus the total displacement over $t\in [1,2].$ Therefore, we can calculate it as follows:

$$
x(2)=x(1)+{\int }_{1}^{2}v(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

Carrying out the computations, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(2) & =e+{\int }_{1}^{2}{e}^{2-t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =e+{[-{e}^{2-t}]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =e+([-{e}^{2-2}]-[-{e}^{2-1}]) \\  & =e+([-{e}^{0}]-[-{e}^{1}]) \\  & =e+(-1+e) \\  & =2e-1\end{aligned}
$$

So the position of the particle at $t=2$ is $x=2e-1.$

question.knowledge_point: Identifying Open and Closed Sets of Real Numbers
question.problem:
Which of the following sets are closed?

I. $[-2,2]$

II. $[3,9]$

III. $[-1,1)\cup (3,4]$
question.worked_solution:
Recall that:

- A set is *open* if it does not contain any of its boundary points. In other words, an open set consists only of the interior points of the set.

- A set is *closed* if it contains **all** of its boundary points. In other words, a closed set consists of all the interior and all the boundary points of the set.

Among the given sets, only $[-2,2]$ and $[3,9]$ are closed because:

- The boundary points of $[-2,2]$ are $-2$, and $2.$ Both of them lie in the set.

- The boundary points of $[3,9]$ are $3$, and $9.$ Both of them lie in the set.

The other set is not closed because $[-1,1)\cup (3,4]$ has a boundary point $1$, which does not lie in the set.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only".

question.knowledge_point: Calculating a Scalar Projection Using Angles and Magnitudes
question.problem: Suppose $|\,p\,|=2$ and the angle between vectors $p$ and $q$ is $\theta =\frac{5\pi }{6}.$ Find the scalar projection of $p$ onto $q.$
question.worked_solution:
Using the formula for the scalar projection, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{q}\,p & =|\,p\,|\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{6}) \\  & =2\cdot (-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}) \\  & =-\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Calculating a Scalar Projection Using Components
question.worked_solution:
Using the formula for the scalar projection, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{b}\,a & =\frac{a\cdot b}{|\,b\,|} \\  & =\frac{{a}_{x}{b}_{x}+{a}_{y}{b}_{y}+{a}_{z}{b}_{z}}{\sqrt{{b}_{x}^{2}+{b}_{y}^{2}+{b}_{z}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{2\cdot 6+(-1)\cdot 2+2\cdot (-3)}{\sqrt{{6}^{2}+{2}^{2}+(-3)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{4}{\sqrt{49}} \\  & =\frac{4}{7}\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{a}\,b & =\frac{b\cdot a}{|\,a\,|} \\  & =\frac{{a}_{x}{b}_{x}+{a}_{y}{b}_{y}+{a}_{z}{b}_{z}}{\sqrt{{a}_{x}^{2}+{a}_{y}^{2}+{a}_{z}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{4}{\sqrt{{2}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+{2}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{4}{\sqrt{9}} \\  & =\frac{4}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{b}\,a-{\text{comp}}_{a}\,b & =\frac{4}{7}-\frac{4}{3} \\  & =4(\frac{1}{7}-\frac{1}{3}) \\  & =4(\frac{3}{21}-\frac{7}{21}) \\  & =-\frac{16}{21}.\end{aligned}
$$
